name: The Terracotta Army (Xi'an)
scope: The buried clay army in the pits east of Qin Shi Huang's tomb mound at Mount Li, outside Xi'an. T1: a farmer digging a well near Xi'an in March 1974 struck a life-size clay soldier -- the first hint of an entire buried ARMY (answer: the Terracotta Army). T2: the pits hold roughly 8,000 warriors plus 130 chariots and ~670 horses, and no two soldiers' FACES are the same -- sculptors worked from about 10 base face-molds, then individualized every one (answer: every face is individualized). Invert: the 8,000 count is the hook, 'each face different' the payoff. T3: the ranks all face EAST in battle formation, standing guard over the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, China's FIRST emperor, to protect him in the afterlife (answer: they guard the first emperor's tomb / face east). T4: the whole army was once painted in bright lacquer colors that curl and flake away within minutes of meeting the dry air, so the gray army we see is the faded ghost of a rainbow one (answer: the vanished lacquer paint). T5: the actual burial mound 1.5 km west has NEVER been opened -- the ancient historian Sima Qian wrote it holds rivers of MERCURY made to flow mechanically, and modern soil tests find abnormally high mercury readings over the mound (answer: the sealed tomb's mercury rivers). Extra rungs available: the two half-size bronze chariots (among the most complex ancient bronzes); pits of bronze water-birds and terracotta acrobats (a whole underground empire, not just soldiers); the emperor began the tomb at age 13 with ~700,000 laborers.
source: Grokipedia (Terracotta Army, checked; direct fetch 403 bot-blocked) corroborated by en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army (discovery 29 Mar 1974 by Yang Zhifa et al.; 8,000 soldiers / 130 chariots / 520+150 horses; 10 base facial forms; Mount Li 1.5 km; Sima Qian mercury account + high soil-mercury readings); Britannica 'Qin tomb'; Smithsonian Magazine.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (the well-digging farmer, the east-facing ranks), never 'What is the Terracotta Army?'. Every answer is a concrete fact about the Mount Li mausoleum site or its artifacts, not about Qin Shi Huang's political career. Dinner-test payoff = the sealed mercury-tomb rung (T5); accuracy rail: frame it as ancient account (Sima Qian) CORROBORATED by real high-mercury soil readings, NOT a proven look inside -- the interior is unexcavated. Label the 'weapons still razor-sharp from chrome plating' claim as DISPUTED if used. Distractors = other Chinese tombs / imperial sites (Ming tombs, the Beijing mounds).
history_overlap: Qin Shi Huang's unification of China and the Qin dynasty are history-bank episodes; keep every rung anchored to the Mount Li mausoleum site and its artifacts, not the emperor's conquests or administration.

name: Xi'an: the walled city at the end of the Silk Road
scope: Xi'an, ancient Chang'an, wrapped in the most complete city wall in China. T1: Xi'an is ringed by a 14-km rectangle of wall so broad (12-15 m across the top) that people ride BICYCLES the full loop around the city on top of it (answer: you can cycle the complete circuit on the wall / the intact 14-km Ming wall, begun 1370). T2: under its old name Chang'an, Xi'an was the eastern STARTING point of the Silk Road -- the caravan route where camel trains set out across Central Asia toward Persia and Rome (answer: the Silk Road began here / eastern terminus). Invert: the 7,000-km route is the hook, 'this was its eastern end' the answer. T3: the Big Wild Goose Pagoda was built in 652 to house Buddhist scriptures the monk Xuanzang carried back on foot from INDIA (answer: it holds the sutras Xuanzang brought from India). T4: Xi'an's Great Mosque, founded by Silk Road traders, is built like a Chinese TEMPLE -- courtyards, tiled roofs, and a minaret shaped like a pagoda instead of a tower (answer: a mosque built in Chinese-temple style). T5: Xi'an served as capital for 13 dynasties over ~1,100 years (Zhou, Qin, Han, Sui, Tang); at its Tang peak Chang'an held about a MILLION people, the largest city on Earth at the time (answer: Tang Chang'an was the world's largest city). Extra rung: the Bell Tower and Drum Tower at the walled city's exact center.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fortifications_of_Xi'an (14 km, begun 1370 on Tang imperial-city foundation, most complete wall in China); National Geographic 'China's other great wall'; TravelChinaGuide / ChinaHighlights on Big Wild Goose Pagoda (652, Xuanzang) and the Great Mosque; Britannica on Chang'an as Silk Road terminus and Tang-era population.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (ride the wall, watch camels leave the gate), never 'What is the capital of Shaanxi?'. Answers are place-facts or creations born there. Dinner-test payoff = the Chinese-temple-style mosque (T4). Lane border: the Silk Road as a TRADE system is history-flavored -- keep the answer the PLACE-fact (Chang'an as the eastern anchor, the wall, the pagoda), not trade economics or Tang court politics. Do NOT seed a food-origin rung (Xi'an biangbiang noodles / roujiamo belong to the cooking bank). Distractors = other walled Chinese capitals (Nanjing, Beijing, Pingyao).
history_overlap: The Silk Road trade network may appear as a history-bank episode; keep rungs on Chang'an-as-place (the terminus, the wall, the pagoda, the mosque), not on the trade system's economics.

name: Beijing: the imperial capital
scope: Beijing's monumental north-south core. T1: at the heart of the city sits the Forbidden City, the largest palace complex on Earth -- around 8,700 rooms behind a 52-m-wide moat and a 10-m wall, where commoners were forbidden to enter for 500 years (answer: the Forbidden City). T2: legend says the palace was built with 9,999-and-a-half rooms -- one short of the 10,000 that belonged to Heaven alone -- so no emperor would out-rank the gods (answer: the 9,999-room legend). Invert: the near-10,000 count is the hook; label it LEGEND vs the real ~8,700. T3: at the round Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests (Temple of Heaven, 1420), the interlocking wooden structure is held together WITHOUT a single nail (answer: built without nails). T4: the Temple of Heaven's curved Echo Wall carries a whisper the length of its circle, and the emperor prayed there as the 'Son of Heaven' at the winter solstice (answer: the Echo Wall). T5: the whole old city is laid on one straight CENTRAL AXIS 7.8 km long -- Bell Tower to Forbidden City to front gate -- a cosmic spine UNESCO named a World Heritage site in 2024 (answer: Beijing's Central Axis). Extra rungs: the HUTONG lanes and siheyuan courtyard homes gridded since the Mongol Yuan era (the word 'hutong' is Mongolian for 'well'); the golden roof-tiles reserved for the emperor; the Summer Palace's Kunming Lake and Long Corridor; the Meridian Gate.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forbidden_City (1406-1420 under the Yongle Emperor; ~8,886 rooms vs the 9,999 legend; 72 ha; 10 m wall, 52 m moat; largest preserved palace complex; residence 1420-1924); Britannica 'Forbidden City'; Association for Asian Studies on number-symbolism; UNESCO 2024 inscription of the Beijing Central Axis; standard sources on the Temple of Heaven (nail-free Hall of Prayer, Echo Wall) and hutong etymology.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (stand in the moat's shadow, walk the axis), never 'What is the largest palace?' or 'What is the capital of China?'. Every answer is a concrete architectural or urban wonder. Dinner-test payoffs = the no-nails Hall (T3) and the 9,999-room legend (T2) -- flag 9,999 as LEGEND against the documented ~8,700. Distractors = other imperial complexes (Seoul's Gyeongbokgung, Kyoto's palaces, Xi'an). Lane border: Ming/Qing dynastic events are history-bank material; keep rungs on the buildings and city form.
history_overlap: Ming and Qing dynastic history (and 1949 events at Tiananmen) belong to the history bank; keep every rung on Beijing's architecture and urban form -- palace, temple, axis, hutongs.

name: Shanghai: the Bund facing the future
scope: Shanghai's Huangpu riverfront, past on one bank and future on the other. T1: along the west bank stands the BUND, a curving row of grand European-built stone banks and hotels from a century ago, so it looks like a slice of London dropped into China (answer: the Bund / the colonial waterfront). T2: directly across the river rises PUDONG -- farmland and warehouses as recently as 1990, now a wall of glass supertowers -- the two banks facing each other like past and future (answer: Pudong, farmland turned space-age skyline). Invert: the 'rice paddies 30 years ago' hook. T3: the tallest of those towers, the Shanghai Tower, TWISTS 120 degrees as it climbs 632 m -- China's tallest building -- its spiral skin shaped to loosen the wind's grip (answer: the Shanghai Tower, the twisting 632-m tower). T4: out to the airport runs the Shanghai MAGLEV, a train with no wheels that floats on magnets and reaches 431 km/h, long the fastest passenger train in regular service (answer: the maglev / magnetic-levitation train). T5: in the old town, the Ming-era Yu Garden folds ponds, rockeries and ZIGZAG bridges into a tiny space -- the bridges are built crooked because folklore held that evil spirits can only travel in straight lines (answer: Yu Garden's zigzag bridges). Extra rung: the Oriental Pearl Tower's stacked spheres.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Tower + Grokipedia (Shanghai Tower, surfaced in search) -- 632 m, 128 floors, tallest in China, twisting form; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_maglev_train (431 km/h, fastest in regular service 2004-2021); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Bund (colonial-era banks facing Lujiazui/Pudong); standard sources on Yu Garden zigzag-bridge folklore.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (stand on the Bund looking across at Pudong at night), never 'What is China's tallest building?'. The past-vs-future contrast is the through-line. Dinner-test payoffs = the maglev (T4) and the twisting tower (T3); label the zigzag-bridge folklore AS folklore. Accuracy rail: say 'China's tallest' (Shanghai Tower is world's 2nd/3rd, not the tallest overall). Colonial-era Bund: state honestly who built it and why (treaty-port trade) without editorializing -- it's a place-fact, not a stance topic. Do NOT seed a food rung (xiaolongbao = cooking bank). Distractors = other skylines/rivers (Hong Kong, named Pudong towers).

name: Hong Kong: the vertical city
scope: A city of towers on a drowned mountain coast. T1: Hong Kong has MORE skyscrapers than any city on Earth -- over 550 towers taller than 150 m -- crammed onto steep slopes because there is almost no flat land (answer: the most skyscrapers of any city). Invert: the 550+ count is the hook. T2: above them all rises Victoria Peak (552 m); the Peak Tram, one of the world's oldest funiculars (opened 1888), climbs a slope so steep the skyscrapers out the window appear to LEAN (answer: the Peak Tram up Victoria Peak). T3: each night the towers around Victoria Harbour fire synchronized colored lights and lasers -- the 'Symphony of Lights,' the largest permanent light-and-sound show in the world (answer: the Symphony of Lights). T4: with so many people on so little land, the demolished Kowloon Walled City once packed about 33,000 residents into a single block -- for a time the densest place humans have ever lived (answer: Kowloon Walled City, the densest place on Earth). T5: Victoria Harbour ('fragrant harbour') is a RIA -- a river valley drowned when the sea rose over a range of hills -- and its deep, sheltered water is exactly why Hong Kong became one of the world's great natural PORTS (answer: a drowned river valley / ria). Teach 'ria.' Extra rung: the Star Ferry crossing the harbour since 1888.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cities_with_the_most_skyscrapers + Guinness World Records (Hong Kong = most buildings 150 m+, 569 as of 2026); en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_Peak (552 m); standard sources on the Peak Tram (1888), the Symphony of Lights, Kowloon Walled City (~33,000 in one block), and Victoria Harbour as a ria.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (look up the leaning towers from the tram), never 'What is the densest city?'. Accuracy rail: TEACH 'ria' before the T5 answer tests it. Dinner-test payoffs = Kowloon Walled City (T4) and the ria-harbour earth-science reveal (T5). Distractors = other dense cities / natural harbours (Shanghai, Singapore, Manhattan, Sydney). Lane border: the 1997 handover and colonial history are history-bank material -- keep rungs on skyline, tram, harbour geology.

name: Pingyao: the frozen Ming city
scope: A complete walled Ming-Qing town in Shanxi. T1: while nearly every old Chinese city tore its walls down, Pingyao kept ITS entire Ming-dynasty wall -- a 6-km rectangle of rammed earth and brick, rebuilt in 1370, still ringing the whole town (answer: an intact Ming city wall). T2: seen from above the town is shaped like a TORTOISE -- two wells for eyes, six gates for the head, tail and four legs -- a lucky form meant to give the city the long life of the turtle (answer: the city is laid out as a tortoise). T3: inside the walls, a shop called Rishengchang opened in 1823 as China's FIRST bank -- a 'draft bank' (piaohao) that let a merchant deposit silver in one city and draw it out 1,000 km away with a paper note, instead of hauling coins past bandits (answer: Rishengchang, China's first bank). T4: because Pingyao's draft banks handled much of the Qing empire's money, this small town was once called the 'Wall Street of old China,' and its gray courtyard streets survive almost unchanged -- a whole walled Ming-Qing town, not a reconstruction (answer: the 'Wall Street of old China').
source: ChinaDiscovery / ChinaGuide / Wikivoyage on Pingyao (wall ~6,163 m, rebuilt 1370 Ming, best-preserved in China; tortoise plan); standard sources on Rishengchang (est. 1823/1824 by Lei Lutai, China's first piaohao draft bank; 'Wall Street of old China').
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (walk the unbroken wall, find the tortoise gates), never 'What was China's first bank?'. Dinner-test payoffs = the tortoise city-plan (T2) and the first-bank (T3). Lane border: the piaohao system is place-anchored here (the building where it began), not a general economics lecture. Distractors = other walled cities (Xi'an, Nanjing) and other 'first' claims. Accuracy rail: 'first modern-style draft bank in China,' not literally the first exchange of value.

name: Seoul: palace city on the world's strangest border
scope: A megacity of 10 million wedged between granite mountains and the planet's most fortified border. T1: at the city's center stands Gyeongbokgung, the 'Palace of Shining Happiness,' built in 1395; guards in bright robes still change at its gate beneath the painted eaves of the throne hall (answer: Gyeongbokgung / the Joseon royal palace). T2: behind the palace, Bukchon Hanok Village is a hillside of traditional tile-roofed HANOK houses -- curved roofs and warm ondol stone floors -- tucked between glass office towers (answer: the hanok houses / ondol-heated tiled homes). T3: only ~50 km north of this city runs the world's most heavily armed border, the Korean DMZ -- a 250-km-long, 4-km-wide strip of mines and fences that has sealed off North Korea since 1953 (answer: the DMZ / Demilitarized Zone). T4: because no one has farmed, built, or hunted inside the DMZ for 70 years, the deadliest border on Earth turned into an accidental WILDLIFE REFUGE, where endangered red-crowned cranes now winter in the no-man's-land between the armies (answer: an accidental wildlife refuge). Invert: the 'deadliest border' hook, the 'wildlife paradise' payoff. T5: Seoul sits in a bowl of granite peaks split by the Han River, and the sacred mountain Bukhansan rises right at the city edge -- making Seoul one of very few megacities with a real mountain-hiking national park inside its limits (answer: a national park mountain, Bukhansan, inside the city).
source: Standard sources on Gyeongbokgung (founded 1395) and Bukchon hanok/ondol; Smithsonian Magazine and Audubon on the Korean DMZ (1953 armistice; ~250 km x 4 km; accidental wildlife refuge; 7 of 15 crane species incl. red-crowned & white-naped; ~6,168 recorded species); standard sources on Bukhansan National Park within Seoul.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led. VISION: name the divided peninsula as a TIMELESS geographic fact (a fortified line across the narrow waist of the peninsula), NOT current-events commentary -- no editorializing on either government. Dinner-test payoff = the accidental-refuge rung (T4); keep ITS answer the PLACE-fact (why the abandoned strip became a refuge), never crane biology (that's the animal bank). Distractors = other palaces / other divided-place borders. Teach nothing false about the DMZ dimensions.
history_overlap: The Korean War itself is a history-bank episode; geography owns the DMZ-as-place (the fortified strip and its accidental wildlife refuge), not the war's events or diplomacy.

name: Gyeongju: the museum without walls
scope: The old Silla capital, an open valley of tombs and temples in southeast Korea. T1: across Gyeongju's parks sit grassy HILLS the size of houses -- but they are not natural hills, they are the 1,500-year-old royal burial mounds of the Silla kings (answer: royal burial mounds, not hills). Invert: 'grassy hills in a city park' hook, 'they're royal tombs' answer. T2: one opened mound, the 'Heavenly Horse Tomb' (Cheonmachong), gave up a golden crown and a painted saddle-flap showing a white winged horse -- the burial goods of a Silla king (answer: Cheonmachong and its gold crown). T3: Gyeongju holds Cheomseongdae, a bottle-shaped stone tower built in the 630s -- the OLDEST surviving astronomical observatory in East Asia -- laid up from about 362 stones for the days of the lunar year (answer: Cheomseongdae, the oldest observatory). Teach 'observatory.' T4: in the hills above, the Seokguram Grotto shelters a serene granite Buddha positioned to catch the FIRST light of sunrise over the East Sea, carved in the 8th century with remarkable geometry (answer: Seokguram's sunrise-facing Buddha). T5: Gyeongju was the Silla capital for nearly 1,000 years (57 BCE-935 CE), and so many tombs, pagodas and temples survive across the open valley that it is nicknamed 'the museum without walls' (answer: 'the museum without walls' / a 1,000-year capital). Extra rung: Bulguksa temple's stone terraces and twin pagodas.
source: World History Encyclopedia & en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheomseongdae (7th c., built under Queen Seondeok 632-647, oldest surviving observatory in East Asia, ~362 stones, 27 layers, 9.17 m); VisitKorea/AtlasObscura on Daereungwon (23 mounds) and Cheonmachong; standard UNESCO sources on Seokguram Grotto and Bulguksa.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (walk among the mounds that look like green hills), never 'What is the oldest observatory in Asia?'. Dinner-test payoffs = the tombs-that-look-like-hills (T1) and Cheomseongdae (T3); TEACH 'observatory' before testing it. The gold crowns are artifacts OF the place, fine as answers. Distractors = other tomb fields / early observatories (Xi'an mounds, the Beijing Ancient Observatory). Lane border: Silla dynastic politics are history-bank material -- keep rungs on the sites and artifacts.

name: Tokyo: the endless city
scope: The largest metropolis humans have ever built, on a three-plate collision zone. T1: at Shibuya Crossing the traffic halts on every side at once and up to 3,000 people surge across from all directions in a single light -- the busiest pedestrian crossing on Earth (answer: Shibuya Crossing / the scramble). T2: Greater Tokyo is the biggest city the world has ever built -- around 37 million people, more than the whole population of Canada, in one continuous metropolis (answer: the world's largest metro area). Invert: 'more people than all of Canada' hook. T3: right at the center, hidden behind a wide moat and stone ramparts, the Imperial Palace occupies the grounds of Edo Castle -- once the largest castle on Earth -- so a ring of forest and water fills the middle of the world's biggest city (answer: the Imperial Palace on Edo Castle's grounds). T4: Tokyo has been leveled and rebuilt twice in a century -- the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake and 1945 firebombing -- because it sits where THREE tectonic plates grind together, one of the most earthquake-prone spots on the planet (answer: a city rebuilt on a three-plate collision zone). Teach the plate-boundary reason. T5: the Tokyo Skytree rises 634 m, the tallest tower in the world, and its height was chosen as a PUN -- 6-3-4 reads 'mu-sa-shi,' the old name of the plain Tokyo stands on (answer: the Skytree, whose height spells 'Musashi'). Extra rungs: Shinjuku Station, the busiest on Earth (~3.34 million riders a day); the Yamanote loop line; Tokyo was called Edo until 1868; much of the bayfront is reclaimed landfill.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Tokyo_Area (~37 million, world's largest urban agglomeration) and en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tokyo; standard sources on Shibuya Crossing volumes, the Imperial Palace on the Edo Castle site, the Tokyo Skytree (634 m / 'Musashi' pun), and the Tokyo region's position at the junction of the Pacific, Philippine Sea and North American/Eurasian plates (1923 Great Kanto quake).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (stand in the crossing, look across the palace moat), never 'What is the largest city?'. Dinner-test payoffs = the Skytree pun (T5) and Shibuya (T1). Accuracy/lane rail: the T4 rung teaches the EARTH-SCIENCE reason Tokyo keeps rebuilding (the plate boundary) -- that's geography's lane; the 1945 firebombing itself is history-bank -- keep the answer the place/earth-process fact. Distractors = other megacities / supertall towers (Shanghai, Seoul, Skytree vs Skytree-rivals).

name: Kyoto: the thousand-year capital of temples
scope: Japan's old capital, a city of ~1,600 temples that WWII spared. T1: the Golden Pavilion (Kinkaku-ji) stands on a still pond wrapped in real GOLD LEAF, its upper floors gilded so brightly they mirror upside-down in the water (answer: Kinkaku-ji, the gold-leaf pavilion). T2: the Kinkaku-ji you see is a 1955 rebuild -- in 1950 a troubled young monk burned the original 1397 pavilion to the ground, a shock so deep the novelist Mishima wrote a famous book about it (answer: it was burned down by a monk in 1950). T3: at Fushimi Inari shrine, THOUSANDS of vermilion torii gates -- about 10,000 -- stand shoulder to shoulder up the mountainside, forming glowing orange tunnels; each was donated by a business praying for good fortune (answer: the tunnels of ~10,000 torii gates). T4: in Arashiyama a grove of giant timber BAMBOO towers overhead so densely that the creaking, hissing wind through the stalks is officially listed among Japan's '100 soundscapes to preserve' (answer: the Arashiyama bamboo grove and its protected sound). T5: Kyoto was Japan's capital for over 1,000 years (794-1868) and holds ~1,600 Buddhist temples and 400 Shinto shrines -- and it came through WWII nearly untouched because US Secretary of War Henry Stimson personally struck it from the atomic-bomb target list to spare its cultural treasures (answer: Kyoto was deliberately spared the bomb). Extra rungs: Kiyomizu-dera's nail-free wooden stage jutting over the hillside; the Gion geisha district; the Philosopher's Path; 17 UNESCO-listed sites.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinkaku-ji and /wiki/Kinkaku-ji_arson (burned 2 July 1950 by novice Hayashi Yoken, rebuilt 1955; Mishima's novel); standard sources on Fushimi Inari (~10,000 torii, Senbon Torii) and the Arashiyama bamboo soundscape; documented Stimson intervention removing Kyoto from the atomic target list.
framing_note: Voice: scene-led / story-led. Dinner-test payoffs = the ~10,000-torii tunnels (T3) and the spared-the-bomb rung (T5). ACCURACY RAILS: label the torii count 'about 10,000' (a commonly cited figure); the Stimson sparing IS documented, but the popular 'he honeymooned in Kyoto' motive is DISPUTED -- frame the cultural-significance reason and flag the honeymoon story as legend. Distractors = other temple cities (Nara, Beijing) / other famous torii (Fushimi vs Itsukushima). Lane border: WWII targeting is history-bank; here it is a place-fact about why Kyoto survives intact.
history_overlap: The atomic-bomb targeting decision belongs to the history bank; geography owns the place-fact that Kyoto survived intact -- keep the T5 rung on the city's preservation, not the war.

name: Nara: the first capital and its Great Buddha
scope: Japan's first permanent capital, where sacred deer roam the streets. T1: in Nara about 1,200 wild sika DEER wander the streets and parks freely, and many have learned to BOW their heads to visitors begging for deer-crackers (answer: the bowing, free-roaming deer of Nara). T2: the deer roam untouched because for over 1,000 years they were revered as sacred MESSENGERS of the god of Kasuga Shrine, so harming one was long a serious crime (answer: they were protected as sacred messengers). T3: Nara's Todai-ji temple holds the Great Buddha (Daibutsu) -- a bronze figure about 15 m tall, cast from roughly 500 tonnes of bronze and dedicated in the year 752 (answer: the Great Buddha of Todai-ji). T4: the hall that shelters it, the Daibutsuden, was for centuries the largest WOODEN building on Earth -- and the version standing today is only two-thirds the width of the even larger original (answer: the world's largest wooden building). T5: Nara, as Heijo-kyo, was Japan's FIRST permanent capital, founded in 710 and laid out on a grid modeled on Chang'an in China -- before it, the capital moved each time an emperor died (answer: Japan's first permanent capital, modeled on Chang'an).
source: Nippon.com 'Vairocana, the Great Buddha of Todaiji' and Todai-ji sources (Daibutsu ~15 m, ~500 t bronze, dedicated 752; Daibutsuden long the world's largest wooden building, now ~2/3 the original width); standard sources on Nara Park's ~1,200 sika deer, the Kasuga-messenger tradition, and Heijo-kyo (capital from 710, grid modeled on Chang'an).
framing_note: Voice: scene-led (deer bowing in the temple courtyard). Dinner-test payoffs = the bowing deer (T1) and the largest-wooden-building (T4). LANE BORDER (important): the deer rungs stay on the PLACE (why the deer roam Nara + the sacred-messenger custom + the learned bow) -- never sika-deer anatomy or biology, which belong to the animal bank. Accuracy rail: the 'two-thirds of the original width' fact is real. Distractors = other Great Buddhas / early capitals (Kamakura's Daibutsu, Kyoto).

name: Hiroshima: the city that came back
scope: The rebuilt city and the single ruin it chose to keep. T1: in the middle of Hiroshima stands a shattered, domed ruin left exactly as it was on 6 August 1945 -- the Atomic Bomb Dome, the only building near the blast's center that kept its shape (answer: the Genbaku / Atomic Bomb Dome). T2: the dome survived because the bomb detonated almost straight OVERHEAD -- about 600 m up and only ~150 m to the side -- so the downward force pressed on its walls from directly above and its steel-and-concrete skeleton stayed standing while everything around it was flattened (answer: the near-vertical overhead blast). Invert: 'why did just THIS building survive?' T3: the domed building was not a monument before the war -- it was a cheerful 1915 exhibition hall designed by a CZECH architect, Jan Letzel, which is why its European dome looked so unlike its neighbors (answer: a Czech-designed 1915 exhibition hall). T4: the ruin was nearly demolished, but Hiroshima chose to freeze it as a Peace Memorial; nearby, a monument buried under thousands of folded paper CRANES honors Sadako, a girl who folded them while dying of the bomb's radiation (answer: the Children's Peace Monument / the paper cranes). T5: trees within a kilometer of the blast -- ginkgos and a weeping willow -- put out fresh buds the very next spring and still grow today; these 'survivor trees' (hibaku jumoku) became living proof that the city, once thought barren for decades, would live (answer: the survivor trees / hibaku trees).
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima_Peace_Memorial + Grokipedia (Hiroshima Peace Memorial, surfaced in search) -- 8:15 a.m. 6 Aug 1945; hypocenter ~150 m horizontal, ~600 m vertical; near-vertical blast preserved the shape; only structure standing near the hypocenter; built 1915, designed by Jan Letzel; preserved 1966, UNESCO 1996; standard sources on the Children's Peace Monument / Sadako and the hibaku survivor trees.
framing_note: VISION: handle with gravity and plain fact -- a real catastrophe, no glib or breezy tone, and NO editorializing on the bombing decision itself (that is the history bank). Geography owns the DOME-as-structure (why it alone survived), the preserved and rebuilt city, and the survivor trees. Dinner-test payoffs = the paper cranes (T4) and the survivor trees (T5), both handled soberly; the T2 rung teaches the overhead-blast reason. Distractors = other preserved ruins / other rebuilt cities. Loading/framing tone throughout must stay respectful.
history_overlap: The atomic bombing (the decision, the weapon, the war) is a history-bank episode; geography owns the dome-as-place, the rebuilt city, and the survivor trees -- keep every rung there and treat the topic soberly.

name: Miyajima: the floating torii
scope: Itsukushima Shrine on the sacred island in Hiroshima Bay. T1: off the shore of Miyajima island stands a giant vermilion TORII gate that at high tide appears to FLOAT on the sea, cut off from land (answer: the floating torii gate). T2: at low tide the water drains away and you can walk out across the flats to stand right beneath the ~16-m gate -- so the same gate is 'in the sea' and 'on dry land' twice a day with the TIDES (answer: the tide reveals it / it's reachable on foot at low tide). Invert with the tide.
